e.t: Abiathar is a personal name, referring to the biblical figure Abiathar. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears once, in Mark 2:26, and it is rendered as “Abiathar.” The word itself identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, this entry explains the name’s ordinary reference, while the precise significance of its use depends on the passage in which it appears.

This word describes a person as “without God.” It identifies someone by their relationship to God, emphasizing the absence expressed by the phrase. It is a description of a person’s condition, not a personal name or an action. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, at Ephesians 2:12. Its basic meaning is clear, while the fuller force of its use depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “each,” referring to individual persons or things considered one by one within a group. It helps distinguish the members of a group without treating them as an indistinguishable whole. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 13 times, with the same basic sense. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the noun or group it describes, but the central idea remains individual attention or distribution among the members.

This Greek New Testament word means “man” and can also mean “husband.” It identifies a male person generally, while the surrounding sentence determines whether the more specific marital sense is intended. Thus, it may refer to a man without speaking about marriage, or to a husband when that relationship is the point. It occurs 216 times in the Greek New Testament, so its ordinary meaning is broad rather than limited to one setting.

e.t: This verb means “to make an orphan of” or “to orphan.” It describes the act of leaving someone in the condition of an orphan, emphasizing what happens to the person rather than naming the person themselves. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Thessalonians 2:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, but its central meaning remains the making of an orphan or the experience of being left parentless.

This word refers to a genealogy—an account of family descent or ancestry. It identifies a record or discussion tracing people through their family lines. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Timothy 1:4 and Titus 3:9. These references show its limited New Testament use, while the word itself points to genealogical matters rather than to a particular person or event. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to wine, specifically sweet wine. It is a noun for a drink made from grapes and is used as a straightforward name for wine rather than as a description of a person, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 2:13. Its basic meaning is therefore narrow and concrete: wine, with sweetness highlighted in the fuller sense. The surrounding verse determines how the word functions in that specific statement.

e.t: This word means “to spend,” referring to using up or giving out something such as money, resources, or personal strength. It describes expenditure rather than simply possessing something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including statements about spending money and spending oneself for others. The exact object being spent is determined by the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains the same: something valuable is used up or devoted. e.t: This word means “to explain” or “to tell.” It is a verb used when someone is asked to make something clear by giving its meaning or account. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Matthew. The word therefore points to clear communication: bringing an explanation or report into understanding. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is straightforwardly explaining or telling something so that others can understand it.

e.t: “From there” points back to a place, situation, or position already mentioned and indicates movement or origin away from it. It functions as a locating expression: the reader is meant to understand that someone came, went, traveled, or acted from that previously identified place. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 27 times, showing regular use for connecting an action with where it began. Its exact force in any verse depends on the place or circumstance supplied by the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Greek verb means “to scorn” or “to spit out,” expressing strong rejection or contempt toward someone. It describes treating a person as utterly unwanted rather than receiving or honoring them. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, at Galatians 4:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a forceful response of rejection and disdain.

me: Verb, Future, Passive, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This word means “to dream” or “to have visions.” It describes receiving or experiencing dreamlike visions, functioning as an action word rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing this sense in two passages. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the experience of dreaming or seeing visions.

e.t: This word means “to agree” or “to consent,” describing a person’s willing acceptance of something. It functions as a verb, expressing the act of agreeing or giving consent rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs ten times. Its central meaning remains consistent, while the surrounding sentence identifies what a person accepts, approves, or agrees to. The word can therefore describe ordinary consent as well as a deliberate acknowledgment expressed through agreement.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to throw on,” describing the act of placing or casting something onto another person or thing. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 19:35 and 1 Peter 5:7. Its basic meaning focuses on the action of putting something on or transferring it onto another. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but the central idea remains a deliberate throwing or placing upon something else.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to accumulate” or “to gather a great number.” It describes bringing things or people together in increasing quantity rather than merely collecting one item. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on assembling a substantial amount or group.

This word means “loss,” describing something suffered as a setback, disadvantage, or defeat. It is a noun that names the result or condition of coming short rather than an action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 11:12 and 1 Corinthians 6:7. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a loss or damaged outcome. The word’s established rendering is also “loss,” supporting this straightforward sense.

Thomas is a personal name, rendered “Thomas.” It identifies the same person mentioned among Jesus’ disciples and in the early church’s list of apostles. The name occurs 11 times in the Greek New Testament, with most occurrences in John’s Gospel. As a name, it does not describe an action, quality, or doctrine by itself; its significance comes from the person it identifies and the surrounding passage. It appears from Matthew through Acts, including three Gospel lists and several references in John.

e.t: This word means “to condemn”—to declare someone guilty or deserving judgment. It describes a decisive judgment against a person, rather than merely noticing or evaluating wrongdoing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, including teachings about condemning others and a statement that the righteous were condemned. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains passing a guilty judgment against someone.

This word means “tax” or “taxes”: money required as a levy by an authority. It is a noun naming the tax itself, not the act of paying it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Matthew and Mark. The basic idea remains consistent: a financial charge identified as tax or taxes, and the surrounding sentence determines how that charge is being discussed.

This word means a lot or lots—something used to make a selection or determine an outcome. In the New Testament, it can refer to the object or method involved in casting lots, as in several accounts surrounding Jesus’ clothing and the choosing of Matthias. It occurs 11 times in 10 New Testament verses, including Acts, the Gospels, Colossians, and 1 Peter. Its exact significance in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Cos is a proper place-name, identifying the location called “Cos” rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 21:1. Its meaning is therefore the name itself: Cos. The supplied lexical information does not provide a broader figurative or symbolic sense, and the verse text is not included here to explain the place’s role in that passage.

Maath is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, at Luke 3:26, and is rendered “Maath.” Because it is a name, its meaning here is primarily the person it identifies; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that individual’s specific place in the text.

This word means “ink” and can also refer to “the color black.” It names the dark writing substance used to put words on a surface, while its broader sense identifies blackness or a black color. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in separate verses. Its clearest ordinary meaning is the material used for writing, though the exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

e.t: This word means “exchanged” or “to exchange”: to substitute one thing for another or alter what was originally in place. It describes an act of replacement rather than merely moving something from one location to another. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Romans 1:25–26. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains an intentional exchange or substitution.

This word refers to a “new convert,” someone who has only recently been converted. It describes a person at the beginning of the faith, rather than someone with long experience. In its one Greek New Testament occurrence, it identifies a recently converted person. The word emphasizes the newness of that conversion and the person’s limited time since becoming a believer; the surrounding verse is needed to understand why that description matters there.

This word means “night” or “nights,” referring to the nighttime period rather than the day. It functions as a noun for the hours of darkness and can identify when something happens. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 61 times, showing that it is a normal word for describing time. Its use ranges across ordinary events, sayings, and prophetic passages, while its basic meaning remains the same: nighttime.

This word means “complete” or “completely.” It describes something as whole, entire, or lacking nothing, and can express the thoroughness of an action or result. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, once in Luke and once in Hebrews. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains total completeness rather than something partial or unfinished.

This word means “dish,” referring to a vessel used to hold or serve food. It is a concrete object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 23:25. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a dish or serving vessel. The word therefore points to something associated with food and table use.

e.t: This word means “fifty,” the number five tens. It identifies a quantity and can refer to people or things counted as fifty, including a group numbered by that amount. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, so its basic meaning remains consistent while the things being counted vary from passage to passage. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding sentence counts or measures. [p03:word:greek-nt:G4004:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G4004:occurrences]

This word means “bird” or “birds,” referring to flying creatures. It is a common noun used in the Greek New Testament for birds generally, without pointing to one particular species. It occurs 14 times in 14 New Testament verses, including passages that speak of birds in ordinary illustrations and comparisons. The plural sense is often reflected when the word refers to birds as a group, while the basic meaning remains the same: a bird or birds. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This Greek New Testament word means “Reu,” the personal name of an individual. It functions as a proper name, identifying someone rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament corpus, at Luke 3:35. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, this entry gives the word’s ordinary naming function without assigning additional meaning or contextual significance to its use.

Rhesa is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name appears once, at Luke 3:27, and is rendered “Rhesa.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes the person being mentioned. The surrounding verse and passage provide the specific role or significance of that person.

This word means a “sign,” an indication that can be recognized as pointing to something. The Greek New Testament uses it as a noun for a sign or signs, whether one sign or more than one. It occurs 77 times in 69 verses, so it is a regularly used New Testament term rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word means “to dwell” or “to live”—to remain in a place as one’s home or continuing presence. It describes an established, ongoing residence rather than a brief visit. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times: once in John and four times in Revelation. Its repeated use centers on the idea of dwelling, while the surrounding passage determines the precise force in each verse.

This word means “pillar,” referring to an upright support or column. It can be used for something that holds up a structure and, by extension, for a person or thing viewed as providing firm support. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Galatians, 1 Timothy, and Revelation. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “agreement”: a state of shared consent or being united in what is accepted. It describes concurrence between parties rather than merely a spoken statement or casual association. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Corinthians 6:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the joining of two sides in common accord.

e.t: This word means “to assemble” or “to come together.” It describes people gathering in one place or joining together, rather than remaining separate. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 30 times, including passages about people gathering around Jesus, meeting with others, or assembling for shared activity. Its exact sense in a particular verse depends on who is gathering and why, but the central idea remains coming together as a group.

This word means “wealth,” referring to material possessions or prosperity. It describes riches as something valuable that can be gained, enjoyed, or lost. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 18:19. The word itself identifies wealth plainly, while the surrounding verse and passage determine how that wealth functions in the immediate statement. Its basic sense remains focused on material riches rather than an abstract quality or spiritual virtue.

This word describes someone who is “past one's prime”—having passed the period regarded as that person's prime. It is a descriptive expression, not a name or title. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 7:36. The word therefore has a narrow documented range in this corpus, and its basic meaning should be kept close to the idea of being beyond one's prime.

This word describes someone who is “thoughtful” and “wise.” It is used of people marked by practical wisdom and sound judgment, rather than merely by knowledge. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times and commonly describes a person whose conduct or choices display wisdom. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a thoughtful, wise person or quality.

This word means “lame,” describing a person whose ability to walk is impaired. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 14 times for people identified by this physical condition. The word appears in Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, and Hebrews, showing a consistent reference to impaired walking rather than a separate spiritual or moral quality. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and sentence.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “from here” or “hence.” It points outward from a stated place, position, or point of reference, expressing where something proceeds or what follows from there. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 17:20 and Luke 16:26. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary sense is a directional expression meaning “from here” or “hence.”
